lesson.title: The Circuit's Friction: Resistance and Ohm's Law
lesson.summary: Introduces resistance as the opposition a material offers to current flow, states Ohm's law relating voltage, current, and resistance, and computes the resistance of a real length of copper wire.
lesson.body:
Every material offers some opposition to the flow of charge through it, and that opposition is called resistance. You already know voltage as the push that drives current and current as the resulting flow of charge, so it is natural to ask how those two quantities relate for a given circuit element. For a very large class of materials and devices, particularly metals at constant temperature, the relationship is beautifully simple: the current through the element is directly proportional to the voltage across it. That proportionality is Ohm's law, written V = IR, where R is the resistance, measured in ohms and symbolized by the Greek letter omega.

Resistance is a property of the object, not just the material, and it depends on geometry as well as composition. A resistor is built from a specific material with a specific length and cross sectional area, and all three factors matter. The governing relationship is R = rho times L divided by A, where rho, the resistivity, is an intrinsic property of the material measured in ohm meters, L is the length of the conductor, and A is its cross sectional area. Longer wires resist more, thicker wires resist less, and different materials resist differently even at identical dimensions.

Copper, the metal used in most household wiring, has a resistivity of roughly 1.7 times 10 to the negative 8 ohm meters at room temperature. Consider 10 meters of copper wire with a cross sectional area of 1 square millimeter, or 1 times 10 to the negative 6 square meters. Its resistance is R = rho L / A = (1.7 times 10^-8 times 10) divided by (1 times 10^-6), which works out to about 0.17 ohms. That is why long extension cords and thin gauge wire cause noticeable voltage drop over distance, while thick, short copper wire is treated as nearly zero resistance in most circuit analysis.

Ohm's law also lets you solve for whichever quantity you do not already know. If a 9 volt battery is connected across a resistor and a multimeter reads 0.02 amps of current flowing, the resistance is R = V / I = 9 / 0.02 = 450 ohms. If instead you know the resistance and current, voltage follows directly as V = IR, and if you know voltage and resistance, current follows as I = V / R. All three forms describe the exact same physical relationship.

Not every device obeys Ohm's law. Diodes, transistors, and light bulb filaments at high temperature all show a nonlinear relationship between voltage and current, meaning their effective resistance changes depending on operating conditions. Devices that do obey V = IR at all reasonable operating points are called ohmic, and resistors are deliberately manufactured to behave this way as reliably as possible across a wide range of voltage and current.

Temperature is one more factor worth keeping in mind. For most metals, resistivity increases as temperature rises, because hotter atoms vibrate more and scatter the flowing electrons more often, which is part of why the thin tungsten filament in an incandescent bulb has noticeably higher resistance once it is glowing hot than it does when cold. Resistors used in precision circuits are sometimes chosen specifically for how little their resistance drifts with temperature, a specification manufacturers list as a temperature coefficient right alongside the nominal ohm value printed on the part.
